title: Throughput regression triage and profiler recipes
body:
Purpose:
This is a lightweight, reproducible checklist and set of profiler recipes for investigating throughput regressions in the serving runtime. Aim: get from alarm -> reproducible control run -> targeted profile -> hypothesis -> remediation proposal within a single on-call/triage session (60–120m).

Context and audience:
- Audience: SREs, bench engineers, runtime devs responsible for throughput SLAs.
- When to use: sudden throughput drop, sustained throughput drift after deploy, or noisy benchmark-to-benchmark variance that blocks claims.

Quick triage checklist (first 15–30m):
1) Capture the failing run artifacts. Collect: loadgen config, run name, run id, exact commit hash, model variant, container tag, and region.
2) Re-run the same control workload at low scale (1 client / 1 concurrency): if the problem reproduces at tiny scale, this is likely a deterministic path (code/arch), else scale-related.
3) Snapshot system state: kubectl describe pods + nodes, docker inspect, nvidia-smi --query, dmesg tail, top -b -n1. Save outputs to ticket.
4) Check telemetry dashboards: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, instance-level GPU utilization, scheduler queue length, host CPU steal, I/O saturation, and recent deploys.
5) Run a golden-run (control) on a pinned known-good commit and compare: throughput, latency histograms, GPU util, and memory.

Sanity checks for load generator and repeatability (10–20m):
- RNG hygiene: ensure entropy seed is fixed for deterministic prompt selection where applicable. For loadgen that uses randomized prompt pick, set SEED env var and record it.
- Client-side pacing: verify inter-arrival distribution (poisson vs constant). Use the same waveform for control and variant.
- Session affinity: if the workload is sessioned (KV cache), make sure client shard mapping is identical across runs.
- Warm start vs cold start: decide and document the warmup policy (see Warmup section).
- Capture client-side metrics (request-times, retries, HTTP-level errors) alongside server metrics.

Controlled experiment layout (recommended minimal matrix):
- Control: known-good commit, N clients, concurrency C, 30–60s warmup, 5–10m steady window.
- Variant: suspect commit, same N/C, identical seed and warmup.
- Repeat: run both control & variant 3 times each (interleaved) to estimate variance.
- If noise is high, increase steady window to 10–15m or add more repetitions.

Warmup strategy (anchored warmup):
- Purpose: stabilize GPU kernels, JIT, and caches.
- Procedure: use a short staircase warmup anchored to the same seed set: 5s at 10% load -> 20s at 30% -> 60s at target. Then wait 10s before measurements.
- Avoid single-shot ramp to target; it creates queuing transients.

Profiler recipes (pick appropriate toolchain):
1) System-level quick profile (5–10m):
   - nvidia-smi dmon (1s) to capture GPU power, temp, mem, smpct.
   - top -H -b -n1 > threads.txt to see CPU thread hotspots.
   - iostat -dx 1 10 to check disks.
   - ss -s and netstat -s for socket states.
2) GPU kernel-level sampling (when throughput drop persists):
   - nsight-sys for end-to-end traces (30–60s). Capture kernel timings, memcpy ops, CPU-GPU sync points.
   - nvprof / CUPTI samplers on older stacks. Record kernels with inclusive/exclusive times.
3) Kernel occupancy and memory pressure:
   - Run perf/cuda-metrics or nvprof sample to check for low SM utilization, long memcpy blocking, or frequent kernel launches.
4) Scheduler/queue contention (runtime-specific):
   - Enable runtime tracing hooks (runtime TRACE=1) to log request queue size, dequeue latencies, and batch assembly times.
   - Capture traces and correlate request timestamp -> kernel start time.
5) Lightweight eBPF trace for syscalls/latency spikes:
   - run bpftrace one-liners to capture slow epoll/wait syscalls.

Load generator config staples (example YAML snippet, adapt to runner):
- NOTE: this is a textual snippet; adapt keys to your runner (proto: http/grpc).

loadgen:
  clients: 4
  concurrency: 8
  seed: 12345
  arrival: poisson
  prompt_set: /mnt/prompts/anchor-1000.json
  warmup: 
    steps:
      - duration_s: 5
        load_pct: 10
      - duration_s: 20
        load_pct: 30
      - duration_s: 60
        load_pct: 100
  steady_window_s: 600
  measurement_window_s: 300
  capture_traces: true

Practical thresholds and signals (heuristic):
- Variance floor: if control run p50 throughput variance > 3% across repeats, increase steady window or number of repetitions.
- Kernel shift: sudden drop in SM utilization (>10pp) with same queue lengths -> likely kernel codepath or input-size regression.
- Memory pressure: higher DRAM bandwidth + higher memcpy times -> consider memory fragmentation or different batching.
- Queuing growth: rising scheduler queue length with flat GPU utilization -> potential scheduling bug or backpressure issue.
- Host CPU saturation: if host CPU > 80% and many context switches, the inference thread scheduling could be the bottleneck.

Naming, artifacts, and reproducibility conventions:
- Run name: YYYYMMDD_tier_commit-model_seed_clientsx_conc (e.g., 20250315_staging_abc123_gpt2q_12345_c4x8)
- Attachments to ticket: loadgen config (yaml), raw telemetry (CSV/TSV), nsight/trace, container metadata, commit hash, and any client logs.
- Archive the seed and the exact prompt slices used.

Hypothesis template (fill for each run):
- Symptom: short description (e.g., 40% throughput drop at p50, p95 unchanged)
- Probable cause: e.g., kernel launch overhead increased due to smaller batch sizes
- Evidence: bullet list of signals from traces/metrics
- Next repro step: short command or script to run
- Risk/impact: services affected, SLA exposure
- Owner and ETA

When to escalate to runtime owners (guideline):
- Reproducible at micro scale (1 client) -> file runtime bug and assign immediately.
- Reproducible only at high concurrency with clear queue growth and trace-based evidence -> SRE + runtime team sync.
- If tracing shows kernel regressions -> runtime + research/compiled kernels triage.

Post-mortem and regression prevention steps:
- Add failing run as a regression test in the bench harness with the same seed and config labeled as flaky/stable depending on variance.
- If root cause is scheduling/architecture, add a microbenchmark that exercises that codepath (fast-feedback).
- Record a short note in the change log for rollouts that touch batching, kernel selection, or scheduler heuristics.

Appendix: quick commands summary (copy-paste friendly)
- Export environment for reproducibility: git rev-parse HEAD > commit.txt; docker inspect $(container) > container.json
- Basic telemetry snapshot: kubectl -n serving logs --tail=200 <pod> > pod.log; nvidia-smi -q -d UTIL,TEMPERATURE -l 1 -f gpu-dmon.txt &
- Local nsight capture (30s): nsight-sys --capture 30 -o /tmp/trace && tar -czf trace.tgz /tmp/trace
- Perf on host: perf record -F 99 -a -g -- sleep 60; perf script > perf.out
- Collect kernel timeline: curl "http://localhost:8080/_internal/trace?window=60s" > runtime-trace.json

Notes and known pitfalls:
- Beware of warmup interplay with caching layers: a warmup that populates a cache may mask regressions in cache miss costs.
- Mixed-precision or quantization changes can shift GPU kernel shapes and change occupancy nonlinearly.
- Noise sources: automated backups, noisy neighbors on shared infra, and scheduling churn due to binpacking. Always check node-level noise if variance is high.

Open items / experiments to run:
- quantify steady-window length needed to reduce variance below 2% for our typical GPT-style workloads (small experiment pending).
- evaluate an anchored-warmup vs continuous-warmup policy for multi-tenant racks.

If you run into something you can't explain in 2 hours, tag the runtime owners and create a reproducible minimal case with the above artifacts.

End of doc.
